generalizedRange: Mountain rainforest of western Hainan Island, southern China
hook: In the 1970s fewer than ten remained. Now seven families sing at dawn.

story.text: The Hainan gibbon is the rarest ape on Earth; every wild one lives in one patch of mountain forest at Bawangling, Hainan Island.
At dawn each family sings a duet — the male leads, the females answer — to mark its territory and bind the group.
Males are jet black with a hairy crest, females golden with a black crown; a family is one male, two females, their young.
Once found across the island, it lost 99.9 percent of its forest range, and by the 1970s fewer than ten remained.
A 2003 census found thirteen in two groups; Kadoorie Farm & Botanic Garden began funding monitoring teams and planting native food trees.
When a July 2014 typhoon landslide cut the canopy, tree climbers strung mountaineering rope across the gap; 176 days later the first gibbon crossed.
In 2021 the forest became part of Hainan Tropical Rainforest National Park, 4,269 square kilometres of mountain.
New groups formed in 2014, 2020, 2022 and 2024; by February 2024 there were 42 gibbons in seven groups.
It remains fragile: new breeding pairs are increasingly related, and a female bears an infant only every three years or so.
To witness the Hainan gibbon is to keep company with a song that nearly fell silent — and with those who climb trees to carry it across.

stats.size: 42–60 cm body · 6–8 kg — no tail, arms longer than legs
stats.lifespan: Unrecorded for the species · kin gibbons to 60 in care
stats.diet: Fruit, about 85% · figs when the dry season bites

reproduction.text: A female first breeds at seven or eight and then bears one infant about every three years, nursing it for two — which is why it took two decades for thirteen gibbons to become forty-two.

insight.text: The Hainan gibbon holds the largest home range of any gibbon — up to ten square kilometres per family — most likely because so few families remain to press against its borders.

programs.title: Hainan Gibbon conservation programme
programs.summary: Funds and trains two gibbon monitoring teams, runs the annual census with Bawangling reserve staff, and plants the gibbons' native food trees from a local nursery.

programs.title: Bawangling branch
programs.summary: Manages the forest where every wild Hainan gibbon lives, replants the fig and bischofia trees the gibbons feed on, and has strung six rope corridors across landslide gaps.
